content.text:
1) Answer

Short answer: You can’t “prove” a politician’s inner attitude toward human rights. What you can do is test whether their official actions knowingly curtailed human-rights safeguards. On the record, James Cleverly, as UK Home Secretary, introduced and steered the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024, and defended its core features. Those features deliberately reduce access to human‑rights protections and international oversight for people facing removal, which multiple authoritative bodies judged incompatible with the UK’s human‑rights obligations. That is strong evidence that, in the asylum context, he prioritised other aims over maintaining human‑rights safeguards.

Evidence (with dates and sources):
- He introduced the Safety of Rwanda Bill on December 7, 2023, and it became law on April 25, 2024. The Government’s own published text records that, under section 19(1)(b) of the Human Rights Act 1998, Secretary James Cleverly stated he was “unable to make a statement” that the Bill was ECHR‑compatible but wished the House to proceed anyway. That is an explicit ministerial acknowledgement that compatibility was doubtful at the point of introduction. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-draft-bill/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-accessible?utm_source=openai))
- The Act instructs all decision‑makers to treat Rwanda as safe and disapplies key parts of the Human Rights Act (sections 2, 3, and 6–9) in relevant decisions, narrowing courts’ ability to apply or remedy Convention rights. Parliamentary debates and constitutional committee analysis confirm this disapplication; the text of the Act also does so. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Lords/2024-02-14/debates/DF3D4002-2381-4691-8E89-54B4F3D90DD2/SafetyOfRwanda%28AsylumAndImmigration%29Bill?utm_source=openai))
- Section 5 of the Act gives a minister the personal discretion to decide whether the UK will comply with urgent interim measures from the European Court of Human Rights (Rule 39); domestic courts must not have regard to such interim measures in Rwanda‑removal cases. The Cabinet Office guidance to civil servants formalised that only a minister decides whether to comply. This weakens an international safeguard designed to prevent irreparable harm. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2024/8/section/5/enacted?utm_source=openai))
- The UK Supreme Court (AAA v SSHD, Nov 15, 2023) had just found there were substantial grounds to believe Rwanda removals posed a real risk of refoulement (breach of the absolute ban on torture/inhuman treatment), making the policy unlawful. Parliament then legislated to deem Rwanda safe and limit courts’ scrutiny. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))
- Authoritative human‑rights bodies publicly assessed Cleverly’s legislation as incompatible with the UK’s obligations:
  - The UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights concluded the Bill was “fundamentally incompatible” with the UK’s human‑rights obligations, highlighting the disapplication of HRA provisions and reduced remedies. ([committees.parliament.uk](https://committees.parliament.uk/committee/93/human-rights-joint-committee/news/199840/legislative-scrutiny-highlights-human-rights-failings-of-rwanda-bill/?utm_source=openai))
  - UNHCR (and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights) stated the Rwanda arrangement and Act were not compatible with international refugee/human‑rights law and would curtail judicial scrutiny and remedies. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/europe/news/press-releases/uk-rwanda-asylum-law-un-leaders-warn-harmful-consequences?utm_source=openai))
  - The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights warned the law undermines judicial independence, limits access to remedies against refoulement, and lets ministers disregard binding interim measures. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/migration-and-refugees/-/serious-human-rights-concerns-about-united-kingdom-s-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))
- While defending the policy in Parliament, Cleverly asserted the Government was “absolutely committed to human rights.” The contradiction between that assertion and the law’s effect is the crux of the criticism. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2023-12-06/debates/5B5B3341-380B-459A-8699-4F4428F053DB/UK-RwandaPartnership?utm_source=openai))

Conclusion: You cannot prove a subjective “disregard,” but there is clear, well‑documented evidence that James Cleverly introduced and advanced a law that (a) narrows domestic human‑rights safeguards, (b) sidelines international oversight, and (c) was assessed by the UK Supreme Court context and leading human‑rights institutions as risking violations (especially refoulement). A fair reading is that, at least in the asylum context, he chose to curtail human‑rights protections to achieve policy goals. He disputes that characterisation, but the protections were objectively reduced. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-draft-bill/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-accessible?utm_source=openai))


2) Sources I considered trustworthy

- Source: GOV.UK (Safety of Rwanda Bill – accessible text incl. section 19 statement)
  [1] Credibility (general): Official UK government publishing platform; primary source for ministerial statements and bill texts.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Contains James Cleverly’s own section 19(1)(b) statement verbatim, establishing his awareness that ECHR compatibility could not be certified. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-draft-bill/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-accessible?utm_source=openai))

- Source: legislation.gov.uk (Safety of Rwanda Act – sections, incl. section 5)
  [1] Credibility (general): The UK’s official statute repository; definitive text of Acts.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Primary text confirming disapplication of HRA provisions and the ministerial discretion over ECtHR interim measures. ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2024/8/section/5?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UK Parliament Hansard
  [1] Credibility (general): Official, verbatim parliamentary record.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Shows Cleverly’s position and the Government’s explanation of disapplying HRA sections; contemporaneous statements. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2024-01-17/debates/5D699C11-620A-4804-97A6-E49E3F870A23/SafetyOfRwanda%28AsylumAndImmigration%29Bill?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UK Parliament Joint Committee on Human Rights (official report and news)
  [1] Credibility (general): Cross‑party parliamentary committee with formal scrutiny role.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Provides detailed, methodologically transparent analysis concluding the Bill is fundamentally incompatible with the UK’s human‑rights obligations. ([committees.parliament.uk](https://committees.parliament.uk/committee/93/human-rights-joint-committee/news/199840/legislative-scrutiny-highlights-human-rights-failings-of-rwanda-bill/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UK Supreme Court (AAA v SSHD [2023] UKSC 42)
  [1] Credibility (general): Highest UK court; primary authority on domestic law.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Primary judgment establishing real refoulement risk in Rwanda, forming the legal context the Act sought to overcome. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights (official page)
  [1] Credibility (general): Independent human‑rights institution of the Council of Europe.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Direct statement explaining how the Act undermines remedies against refoulement and allows ministers to ignore interim measures. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/migration-and-refugees/-/serious-human-rights-concerns-about-united-kingdom-s-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UNHCR – official pages and statements
  [1] Credibility (general): UN refugee agency; technical lead on refugee law and protection standards.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Direct UN assessments that the Rwanda arrangement and the Act are not compatible with international refugee law and reduce judicial scrutiny/remedies. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/europe/news/press-releases/uk-rwanda-asylum-law-un-leaders-warn-harmful-consequences?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Law Society of England and Wales (briefing)
  [1] Credibility (general): Statutory professional body for solicitors; non‑partisan legal analysis.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Clear technical summary of how the Act disapplies HRA provisions and restricts courts’ role. Used as a secondary explainer alongside primary texts. ([lawsociety.org.uk](https://www.lawsociety.org.uk/en/topics/immigration/seven-things-you-should-know-about-the-safety-of-rwanda-act?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Reuters (news wires on UNHCR court evidence)
  [1] Credibility (general): International wire service with strong editorial standards.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Corroborates that UNHCR continued to give evidence of ongoing refoulement risks in Rwanda in 2024 litigation. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/rwandas-asylum-system-still-inadequate-un-refugee-agency-tells-uk-court-2024-06-10/?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources I considered not trustworthy (for proof, without independent corroboration)

- Source: The Sun
  [1] Credibility (general): UK tabloid; strong editorial framing; variable rigor on complex legal matters.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Acceptable for quotes/colour but not for proving legal compatibility or human‑rights impacts. I did not rely on it for substantive claims without primary corroboration. ([thesun.co.uk](https://www.thesun.co.uk/news/26798262/james-cleverly-house-of-lords-rwanda/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: GB News
  [1] Credibility (general): Opinion‑led broadcaster; coverage often polemical; not a primary legal source.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Used only to understand political reactions; not suitable to evidence legal propositions about human‑rights compliance. ([gbnews.com](https://www.gbnews.com/politics/richard-tice-council-of-europe-human-rights-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Wikipedia (page on the Act)
  [1] Credibility (general): Useful tertiary overview; accuracy varies; not a primary source.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): I treated it as a lead‑in and verified each relevant claim against primary law, Hansard, and official analyses before relying on it. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_of_Rwanda_%28Asylum_and_Immigration%29_Act_2024?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Individual newspaper editorials/op-eds (e.g., Le Monde editorial)
  [1] Credibility (general): Respected newspaper; editorials are opinion pieces.
  [2] Trustworthiness (this prompt): Useful to understand viewpoints, but not evidentiary for proving legal incompatibility; I used official documents and institutional analyses instead. ([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/opinion/article/2024/04/25/immigration-the-uk-s-shameful-rwanda-law_6669508_23.html?utm_source=openai))

If you want, I can compile direct quotations of the specific statutory subsections that disapply the Human Rights Act and the exact wording of section 5 on ECtHR interim measures, with line-by-line references.
